Title: RM6.7m boost for Indian community
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  Putrajaya has allocated RM6.7 million under the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit  to empower the Indian community through education, entrepreneurship and support for religious institutions.
Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan said the Madani Tuition Programme, Uyarvu Madani and Dharma Madani are important initiatives for the community's holistic development and economic growth.
"We want to see more Indian youths succeed in their studies. We want to see more Indian entrepreneurs successfully expand their businesses to the next level, and we want to see temples remain as institutions that  unite and empower the community," he said at the grant presentation ceremony here yesterday.
Under the Madani Tuition Programme, 2,343 Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia  and Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia  candidates will receive free tuition to ease their families' financial burden.
The classes, which start this month,  will run until  December at 28 selected tuition centres across seven states.
Under the first round of the Uyarvu Madani grant programme, 128 entrepreneurs from various sectors, including food and beverage, cleaning services and barbering, received grants totalling RM3.05 million this year.
"Seventy recipients, or 55 per cent of the total, are women entrepreneurs," he said, adding that the figure demonstrated the resilience and strength of Indian women in business.
He said the grants are for existing and profitable businesses vetted by Putrajaya to help them expand.
"They are already making money. It is just that they cannot grow due to certain constraints."
The grants are channelled through three categories — Micro, Growth and High Growth — with eligible entrepreneurs receiving up to RM50,000, depending on their category.
Ramanan said 91 entrepreneurs received grants under the Micro category, 29 under Growth and eight under High Growth.
The Dharma Madani programme yesterday channelled RM1.04 million to 52 Hindu temples, bringing the total number of recipients to 676 temples.
Putrajaya needs to channel aid to 1,000 temples to achieve its target and utilise the  RM20 million allocation for the initiative.
Ramanan said: "I have high hopes that all recipients will manage these allocations with full integrity, accountability and responsibility so that the target groups can benefit from them and that they have a lasting positive impact on the community."

Title: Malaysia targets RM85.2bil energy savings by 2035 [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia expects its National Energy Efficiency Action Plan 2026-2035 (NEEAP 2.0) to generate RM85.24 billion in cumulative utility savings by 2035, as it seeks to contain energy demand amid rapid industrial expansion and the shift to cleaner power.
The plan targets an 11.6 per cent reduction in national energy demand, equivalent to cumulative energy savings of 815,382 terajoules (TJ) against a business-as-usual scenario, Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said.
The energy-efficiency measures are also expected to prevent 26,108 kilotonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (ktCO2eq) in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, he said.
The targets come as Malaysia faces rising electricity demand from data centres, manufacturing and other energy-intensive industries, while pursuing a broader transition toward renewable energy and a lower-carbon economy.
"Over 10 years, the first NEEAP delivered electricity savings of 60,886 gigawatt-hours (GWh), exceeding its target of 52,233 GWh," he said at the 7th International Sustainable Energy Summit (ISES) 2026 today.
"This is equivalent to an estimated reduction of 35.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent and savings of approximately RM16.1 billion," Akmal said.
NEEAP 2.0 complements the National Energy Policy 2022-2040, the National Energy Transition Roadmap, the New Industrial Master Plan 2030 and the 12th and 13th Malaysia Plans.
The action plan focuses on four strategic thrusts, covering energy efficiency implementation, workforce reskilling and upskilling, sustainable funding mechanisms, and private-sector initiatives and investments.
Key initiatives cover energy efficiency across the industrial, building and domestic sectors, alongside wider adoption of digital technologies and smart energy-management systems.
Akmal said improving energy efficiency was necessary as Malaysia expands clean energy supply, with NEEAP 2.0 aimed at making efficiency an integral part of the economy.
He said the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Act marked an important shift towards institutionalising energy efficiency across the economy.
"Together with the next phase of national policy, including thermal energy management, it will encourage users to optimise consumption, improve competitiveness and reduce pressure on the grid.
"Energy efficiency must become standard business practice and a national productivity tool, and ultimately, a way of life," he said.
Malaysia's 2026 FiT bids to drive RM4.3bIL renewable energy investment
Akmal said Malaysia's 2026 Feed-in Tariff (FiT) e-bidding exercise is expected to catalyse about RM4.3 billion in investment in biogas, biomass and small hydropower projects, as the government seeks to accelerate renewable energy deployment and strengthen domestic supply chains.
He said the awarded projects would also generate about RM617 million in demand for locally manufactured gas engines and boilers, creating spillover benefits for domestic manufacturers.
The projects are expected to create about 7,738 indirect jobs while supporting local supply chains and generating wider economic activity, he said.
"This is the outcome we seek. More renewable energy, stronger domestic supply chains, greater investment and tangible economic value for the country," he said.
Under the FiT mechanism, renewable energy producers are paid a fixed tariff for electricity supplied to the national grid over an agreed period. The mechanism provides longer-term revenue visibility for developers and is designed to encourage investment in renewable power projects.
The Sustainable Energy Development Authority Malaysia (SEDA Malaysia) received 48 applications under the latest e-bidding exercise, representing a combined net export capacity of 370.48 megawatts (MW).
Following evaluation, 42 applications with a total approved capacity of 331.355 MW were awarded, Akmal said.
The successful bids comprise 16 biogas projects with a combined capacity of 26.185 MW, 11 biomass projects totalling 135.94 MW and 15 small hydropower projects totalling 169.23 MW.
The implementation of new renewable energy projects under the FiT mechanism is part of the Energy Transition and Water Transformation Ministry's (Petra) commitment to increase renewable energy's share of the country's electricity supply mix to 70 per cent by 2050.
The expansion of biogas, biomass and small hydropower capacity is also expected to strengthen electricity supply reliability by diversifying renewable energy generation sources while providing firm and consistent electricity supply.
Akmal said the outcome demonstrated the government's efforts to expand renewable energy while attracting investment and strengthening local supply chains.

Title: Of MMC Ports, Strait of Malacca and Sultan Ahmed's appointment
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: MORE than six centuries ago, merchant ships from China, India, Arabia and the Malay Archipelago sailed through the Strait of Malacca to one of the busiest trading ports of its time.
At the centre of the Malacca Sultanate's thriving port was the Shahbandar, who managed arriving ships, collected taxes, settled trade disputes and dealt with merchants from different parts of the world.
The ships are different today. They carry containers filled with semiconductors, vehicles, food and components for global supply chains, alongside crude oil and liquefied natural gas.
But the business of ports still comes down to something quite basic: the faster and more efficiently cargo moves, the more attractive the port becomes to global trade.
Malaysia has spent decades building that capability.
MMC Port Holdings Bhd (MMC Ports) now operates the country's largest port network, which handled more than 20 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in 2025.
It is entering its next phase just as the Strait of Malacca is becoming even more important to geopolitics, trade and global supply-chain security.
Why The Strait Matters To Malaysia
The Strait of Malacca connects the Indian and Pacific oceans and remains one of the busiest shipping routes in the world.
Disruptions in the Red Sea and tensions in the Middle East have shown how quickly trouble along a major maritime route can ripple through global trade.
Malaysia has plenty at stake
Apex Securities Research estimates that about 48 per cent of Malaysia's total trade in 2025 was transported by sea.
A major disruption to shipping through the Strait of Malacca could affect as much as 36.8 per cent of the country's total trade.
Under a severe disruption scenario, Malaysia's economic growth in 2027 could slow to between 2.5 per cent and 3.1 per cent, with inflation potentially rising above three per cent.
That is why ports matter beyond the companies running them.
More ships and cargo passing through Malaysian ports mean more business for logistics companies, warehouses, hauliers, ship repairers, technology providers, insurers and financial institutions.
It also means jobs, tax revenue and opportunities for thousands of small and medium enterprises linked to the supply chain.
PTP Changed The Game
For MMC Ports, much of the story begins in Johor.
In 2001, MMC Corp Bhd acquired a controlling stake in the Port of Tanjung Pelepas (PTP), which was developed as an alternative transshipment hub to Singapore.
PTP became the cornerstone of MMC's port expansion.
The group subsequently built a network encompassing Johor Port, Northport in Port Klang, Penang Port and Tanjung Bruas Port.
Today, MMC Ports operates PTP, Northport, Johor Port, Penang Port, Tanjung Bruas Port, Andaman Port, Port Klang Cruise Terminal and Langkawi Cruise Terminal.
In 2025, the network crossed 20 million TEUs for the first time.
PTP remains its most important container hub. It became the first Malaysian port to cross 13 million and then 14 million TEUs within a year.
Northport handled a record 3.80 million TEUs, while Johor Port reached 1.08 million TEUs.
PTP is expanding further through Berth Zero, with 11 additional quay cranes capable of serving ultra-large container vessels and 41 electric rubber-tyred gantry cranes.
Johor Port has also completed two new jetties to increase liquid-cargo capacity.
The next push is digital. MMC Ports is working with NIZE Technology Co. Ltd, the technology arm of Shanghai International Port Group (SIPG), on a five-year Digital Master Plan covering automation, data management, digital twin technology and artificial intelligence.
Then Came Sultan Ahmed
The next development was far less predictable.
Former DP World chairman and chief executive officer Sultan Ahmed Bin Sulayem was appointed executive chairman of MMC Ports following the departure of Datuk Azman Shah Mohd Yusof as group CEO.
The appointment caught the industry by surprise.
Sultan Ahmed is not simply another port executive.
Over more than four decades, he helped turn DP World from a Dubai port operator into one of the world's biggest port and logistics groups, with operations across dozens of countries.
According to an industry source familiar with the development, news that Sultan Ahmed was joining MMC Ports left several players in Singapore's maritime industry "taken aback."
There is a reason for that reaction.
The man who helped build DP World into a global port giant is now leading Malaysia's largest port operator, adding another dimension to the long-running competition between Malaysia and Singapore for transshipment business in the Strait of Malacca.
One man cannot transform a port overnight. But shipping is also a relationship business.
Connections with global shipping lines, reputation and decades of international experience can open doors that are difficult to put on a balance sheet.
Sultan Ahmed's story is also closely tied to Dubai's transformation.
Five decades ago, Dubai was nowhere near the trade, logistics and financial centre it is today.
Jebel Ali Port, free-trade zones and an expanding logistics network helped turn the emirate into a gateway linking Asia, Europe and Africa.
Sultan Ahmed was part of that transformation through DP World, overseeing its expansion through acquisitions and investments across the globe.
His experience was not confined to ports.
He was also involved in Dubai's property development through Nakheel, the developer behind Palm Jumeirah, The World Islands and other large-scale projects that changed Dubai's physical and economic landscape.
That background matters.
It means he comes to MMC Ports with experience not only in running ports, but in seeing how ports, logistics, trade and urban development can work together to create a larger economic ecosystem.
MMC Ports, meanwhile, has already built the network.
The question now is how much more value Malaysia can extract from it.
The Next Contest In The Strait
Malaysia has geography on its side, but geography does not guarantee cargo.
Shipping lines look at cost, efficiency, turnaround time, technology and connectivity before deciding where their ships call and where containers are transferred.
Singapore remains the region's dominant transshipment hub. Other Asian ports are spending heavily on new capacity and automation.
Malaysia is not starting from scratch.
It has MMC Ports' nationwide network, PTP as a major Southeast Asian transshipment hub, growing container volumes and a digital transformation programme already under way.
Now it also has Sultan Ahmed.
He arrives at a very different stage of MMC Ports' development. The network has been built. The volumes are there. Billions have been invested in infrastructure.
The next battle is about productivity, technology, shipping connections and winning a bigger share of trade moving through one of the world's most important waterways.
Whether Sultan Ahmed can repeat in Malaysia what he helped achieve in Dubai is impossible to know at this stage.
But one thing has already happened. The regional maritime industry is watching.
*The writer is a senior lecturer at UiTM's Faculty of Management and Business.

Title: Car bomb kills Haftar intel chief in Libya
Article:
TRIPOLI: The head of military intelligence for the Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls the east and parts of southern Libya, has been killed in a car bombing, the army said in a statement Tuesday.
Fawzi al-Mansouri was assassinated on Monday when an explosive stuck to his car detonated as he was leaving a local mosque at night, the statement said.
Reports said the killing occurred in the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi.
Libya has remained divided since being plunged into war during the ousting in 2011 of former leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival in Benghazi backed by military commander and LNA chief Khalifa Haftar.
Khaled Haftar, the son of Khalifa, told AFP in a statement that an investigation was opened, adding that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic."
"Terrorism is a project targeting the entire region, not just Libya," the statement added.
The bombing was a setback to efforts by the Haftars to paint a picture of stability in the areas they control.
"An attack of this sophistication in an LNA stronghold is also a major blow to the group's security credentials," Hamish Kinnear, an analyst with UK-based Verisk Maplecroft, told AFP.
- REUNIFICATION DEAL -
"The intelligence required to target such a high-profile figure successfully is indicative of significant capabilities on the part of the responsible actor," Kinnear added.
Authorities have yet to identify the perpetrators.
In a statement, the LNA said it would "not cease fighting terrorism and will continue our struggle for the stability and security of Libya, as well as for the unification of its institutions."
Al-Mansouri's killing also came as efforts were under way to unify the country's executive powers under a Washington-mediated plan that the LNA has publicly backed.
"None of this bodes well for a US plan to re-unify Libya," Kinnear said, adding that under the roadmap, neither side "is likely to be satisfied with their respective positions for long."
"A new, destabilising power struggle could soon emerge."
Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui said the killing would "disrupt, or at the very least delay" the US-brokered deal.
"The agreement rests on two premises: that security reigns supreme in Benghazi, and that for senior officers, loyalty to Saddam (Haftar's son and heir apparent) guarantees protection in the Benghazi stronghold," Harchaoui explained.
But "a bomb that kills the head of military intelligence as he leaves a mosque undermines these premises," he said.
- PROMINENT LNA FIGURE -
Meanwhile, reunification would "require some gestures of openness toward reform and change within the army", Harchaoui added.
The Tripoli-based government issued a statement denouncing a "terrorist attack" against al-Mansouri, saying it condemned the killing "regardless of one party's positions or alliances."
Khaled's office later said in a statement to AFP that authorities arrested a "terrorist cell in Benghazi that was preparing to carry out acts of sabotage" but did not say whether it was linked with al-Mansouri's killing.
Authorities in Benghazi held al-Mansouri's funeral on Tuesday afternoon, publishing photos that showed armed men in military fatigues with the attendance of senior LNA officials at the ceremony, including Khaled and Saddam Haftar.
The LNA described al-Mansouri as a "heroic martyr."
Al-Mansouri was a prominent military leader with close ties to the Haftar family.
He played a key role in the LNA's fighting against groups, including the Islamic State, between 2014 and 2017 in parts of the country's east.
He was also a leading figure during Haftar's Russia-backed offensive to seize Tripoli in 2019, which was thwarted by forces in the capital with the support of Turkiye.-AFP

Title: Total solar eclipse to spellbind Europe
Article:
BURGOS, Spain: Millions of Europeans will contemplate the sky in awe on Wednesday as a rare total solar eclipse crosses part of the continent and plunges a swathe of Spain into eerie daytime darkness.
The shadow cast when the Moon blots out the Sun will begin in Russia's remote Arctic north at around 1700 GMT and continue in an arc over Greenland and Iceland.
In Spain, where the total eclipse will be best viewed, the shadow will cross the country diagonally from the northern Atlantic coast to the Mediterranean Sea, where it will vanish at around 1830 GMT.
Far more observers will see a partial eclipse, visible in most of Europe, Canada, the northern United States and northwest Africa.
This will be mainland Europe's first total eclipse since 2006.
Throughout human history eclipses have stirred amazement, fear and reverence, as they appear to momentarily halt the normal course of nature.
The shadow cast by the alignment of Sun and Moon creates a strange twilight during which temperatures drop, shadows appear at strange angles and some animals go to sleep.
But the phenomenon is fleeting: for observers in Spain, the total eclipse will last less than two minutes just before sunset.
It will last slightly longer in parts of Russia and Greenland, though still under two-and-a-half minutes.
The partial eclipse – which occurs as the Moon starts and finishes crossing the Sun's path – will last around one hour and 45 minutes.
The phenomenon will present scientists with a rare opportunity to study the Sun's atmosphere and its outermost layer, as they seek to uncover secrets about solar winds and our star's magnetic field.
- ECLIPSE FEVER -
Eclipse chasers will rush to secure a vantage point with an unimpeded sight of the setting Sun and pray for the dissipation of any clouds, dust or smoke.
Rain and clouds were forecast to spoil the occasion in the Westfjords region of northwestern Iceland, while Reykjavik, the capital, was set to experience its first total eclipse since 1433.
Further south, the Madrid-based AEMET weather agency has predicted clear skies for most of Spain, with a few exceptions in northern and eastern areas.
Eclipse fever is gripping the country, with the type of glasses certified to safely view the Sun hard to find in some places.
The country is banking on eclipse-driven tourism for an economic boost, especially in rural, northern regions that have suffered decades of population decline.
The net contribution to the economy is forecast to be 347 million euros (US$400 million), with more than 446,000 extra tourists visiting the key areas affected by the eclipse, according to the economy ministry.
Sleepy villages that would normally never feature in a typical tourist itinerary have suddenly found themselves inundated with eclipse hunters from around the world.
In Benavente, a small northwestern town that is expected to offer excellent views of the total eclipse, accommodation options have run out.
"We're getting 50 calls a day to ask about where to stay, where to see it, where to park," Benavente tourism office worker Laura del Teso told AFP.
Benavente had "never" had so many foreign tourists, including visitors from Belgium, Britain, Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands and Germany, she added.
- HAZARDS ON HORIZON -
The expected rush has caused trepidation for the authorities, who are pleading for caution amid fears that the heavenly phenomenon will unleash hell on the ground.
Temperatures are expected to exceed 35C Wednesday in most of mainland Spain and could climb above 40C in parts of the northeast, posing health risks for those spending hours outdoors.
AEMET also forecasts a "very high" or "extreme" wildfire risk for much of the country – with the risk amplified by thousands of people occupying parched countryside and clogging small rural roads with their cars.
Officials expect there to be as many as 1.5 million extra road journeys towards the band of totality.
Municipalities have set up dedicated observation points and beefed up security, emergency and transport resources in the hope of managing the mayhem during mainland Spain's first total eclipse in more than a century.
Another total eclipse will cross southern Spain and northern Africa in August 2027, while an annular eclipse – when the Moon is not big enough to completely blot out the Sun, creating a so-called "ring of fire" – is due to visit the Iberian Peninsula in 2028.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Access to justice: Reflections from a mobile court
Article:
THE journey to Kampung Tibabar  was an endurance test in itself. The road was a gruelling stretch of bumpy, loose gravel and jagged stones that shook the vehicle and our modern sensibilities, long before we reached the destination.
I looked at the speedometer of my vehicle. The gravel road alone clocked 8km. With every mile deeper into the interior, our mobile phone signals flickered, weakened and finally died. We were slipping off the grid, crossing an invisible line where urban convenience ends and isolation begins.
We had arrived to set up a mobile court, a temporary lifeline at Kampung Tibabar, located in the district of Ranau, Sabah. Inside the community hall, tables for various government agencies coordinated under the judiciary's initiative were hastily arranged, including, among others, the National Registration Department, Attorney-General's Chambers, Legal Aid Department and Welfare Department, bringing vital assistance directly to the door-step of people who rarely see it.
But amid the bustle of folding tables, forms and officials, what struck me most wasn't the logistics. It was the people.
Villagers arrived clutching worn books and thick files of documents, holding onto these tattered papers like lifelines. Sitting on rows of plastic chairs and waiting patiently in the heat were families, large households of children and elders bearing the quiet, weathered faces of those hardened by the obstacles of daily survival.
As the day unfolded, the gravity of their reality set in. Here were people navigating life without stable Internet, reliable infrastructure or the basic amenities we take for granted.
At the front row sat a young mother trying to soothe a restless, crying toddler in her arms. She looked exhausted, her posture slumped under the weight of hardship, yet she maintained a gentle, patient focus on her child.
Beside her, an elderly lady stood balanced on a single wooden crutch, having lost one leg, yet she had made her way to the hall regardless, unwilling to let it stand between her and the help she came for.
It was a poignant juxtaposition: the official machinery of the state trying to regulate lives through paperwork, sitting just feet away from a mother simply trying to comfort her child with the only warmth she had left, and an elderly woman whose quiet determination spoke louder than words.
The bureaucratic hurdles were heartbreakingly stark. Among the most pressing issues was something as fundamental as the registration of births.
Families grappled with the absence of official paperwork, documents that anchor a person to society, granting them access to education, healthcare and legal identity. Without a birth certificate, a child is practically invisible to the system, locked out before their life has even truly begun.
[[nid:1509211]]
Present at the event were the court magistrates, dedicating their weekend for the community to carry out duties that would otherwise require a trip to the courthouse. These included endorsing late registration of birth, handling matters relating to statutory declarations and signing as commissioner for oaths.
For many rural or underserved communities, these are services that had remained out of reach, not due to unwillingness, but due to the practical barriers of distance, cost and unfamiliarity with formal processes. The nearest court or government office may be hours away, and the cost of travel, time off work or navigating bureaucratic processes can be enough to permanently deter people from resolving even simple legal matters.
The endorsement of late birth registration carried particular significance. Once settled on the spot, individuals could proceed immediately to NRD to apply for their MyKad, a document essential for accessing healthcare, education, employment, and virtually every other form of civic participation.
For those who had gone years, sometimes decades, without formal identification, this single day's proceedings could resolve a barrier that had followed them their entire lives.
A magistrate, after carefully reviewing and considering the testimony and documentation before them, may reject the application if it is found to be unsatis-factory, be it due to insufficient documentation, unreliable witnesses brought to attest to the applicant's identity, parentage, or date of birth and blatant inconsistencies which are not satisfactorily explained by the applicant.
In such cases, applicants are allowed to gather further evidence or produce more credible witnesses before the matter could be reconsidered.
By stepping outside the courtroom and into the community, the judiciary demonstrated that access to justice is not merely about the existence of laws and institutions, but about ensuring people can actually reach them.
Standing there, watching the contrast between the sharp, efficient tools of the mobile court and the deep-seated vulnerability of the villagers, a heavy question crept into my mind:
What does the future hold
for them?
Later, as we visited the village school — SK Tibabar, part of the MyC2C (Dari Mahkamah ke Bilik Darjah) programme's outreach, the heavy cloud of sorrow lifted just enough to let the light through.
In true
rasa tamu
fashion, the students' dance performance turned strangers into honoured guests, wrapping us in a welcome as vivid as it was heartfelt. Their bright eyes and eagerness to learn offered a powerful counterweight to the day's hardships. As our visit came to a close, the school choir gathered to send us off, singing
Lambai
. Their voices carried the vibrant, rhythmic warmth of Sabah, lingering in the air and filling the room with a profound sense of grace.
What unfolded that day was a reversal of how justice is typically delivered. Far removed from the grandeur of the Palace of Justice in Putrajaya, it went looking for the people, instead of waiting for them to come find it.
Access to justice is not an abstract ideal reserved for courtrooms and legal texts; it is measured in birth certificates issued, MyKads made possible, and lives no longer left unrecognised by the state. Justice that waits is justice denied. It must go to them. We will go to them.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: North Korea fires ballistic missile over Sea of Japan
Article:
SEOUL: North Korea fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early Wednesday, Seoul's military said, just days before the planned start of massive US-South Korea joint drills.
"Our military detected at around 6am (2100 GMT Tuesday) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea," the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters, referring to a body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
Japan's Defence Ministry said on social media that the suspected ballistic missile had "already fallen", without providing further details.
Joint exercises between South Korea and the United States lasting 11 days are due to start on Monday, a regular fixture of the summer calendar designed to steel them for defence against the nuclear-armed North.
Pyongyang bristles at the drills – calling them rehearsals for an invasion – and has in the past staged pointed test missile launches before and after the exercises.--AFP

Title: SWCorp investigates alleged Singapore construction waste dumped in Pontian [WATCH]
Article:
PONTIAN: Johor will set up a multi-agency task force to conduct a comprehensive investigation into allegations that construction waste from Singapore was dumped at several locations here.
State Housing and Local Government Committee chairman Datuk Mohd Jafni Md Shukor said the task force would comprise local authorities, police, the district office and the Solid Waste Management and Public Cleansing Corporation (SWCorp).
He said the move was necessary to establish the facts behind the allegations and determine whether the activity was still taking place.
"I have received reports on the alleged dumping, including in Sungai Karang, here, and several other areas, but investigations are still ongoing.
"I understand that the operation involving the dumping of construction waste from Singapore in the area has stopped, but the matter cannot end there."
Jafni said any waste brought in from Singapore and dumped in Johor without the necessary permits or approvals should not be allowed.
"Those carrying out activities in violation of the law will face action. We will not compromise on this matter.
"If waste is brought from Singapore and dumped in Johor without the necessary permits or approvals, action must be taken so that this does not become a cause for concern among Bangsa Johor and the people," he said.
He said coordinated enforcement was also crucial to prevent a recurrence and safeguard residents and the state's environment.
The move follows reports that convoys of trailers allegedly carrying construction waste from Singapore had been travelling to Pontian for dumping for the past two years.
Residents claimed that the heavy vehicles travelled at night and into the early hours, with alleged dumping activities reported in Parit Sikom, Batu 26 Jeram Batu-Pengkalan Raja, Kampung Parit Rambai, Kampung Sungai Dinar and Mukim Sungai Karang.
They also claimed that the heavy vehicles had caused road hazards, with debris allegedly falling onto village roads and resulting in accidents involving motorcyclists.
Residents had questioned how trailers allegedly carrying the waste could pass through the border before using village roads to reach suspected privately owned dumping sites.
Earlier yesterday, Kepong MP Lim Lip Eng called on authorities to explain how construction waste allegedly brought in from Singapore entered Pontian.
"Trailers ferrying waste have a record at the Singapore-Johor border, and authorities must identify who inspected the cargo, checked the documents and authorised the vehicles to enter Malaysia," he said, adding that action should be taken against those found negligent or failing in their duties.

Title: Trump smuggled off Air Force One in secret Iran threat escape
Article:
WASHINGTON: A secret operation that reportedly smuggled Donald Trump off Air Force One in a catering truck before the plane departed carrying journalists and top aides at apparent risk of an Iranian strike has raised questions over US security practices.
The Washington Post reported Monday that Trump covertly exited the presidential plane while it was on the ground in Turkiye on July 8 as his security team deployed a scheme to evade an assassination threat.
Some traveling media expressed anger at having unwittingly served as decoys, while others complained about deception and lack of communication from the White House.
Trump boarded the presidential jet in full view of video cameras and photographers, with AFP pictures showing two supply containers on hydraulic lifts at the front and rear of the aircraft.
But he then reportedly quickly left the plane, stepping inside one of the cargo containers, to board a smaller US Air Force aircraft positioned nearby.
About a dozen journalists traveling in a separate section of Air Force One with no access to the president were unaware of the switch and flew out of Turkey on the plane despite the apparent threat from Iran, which is at war with the United States.
- SHOULDER-TO-AIR MISSILE THREAT? -
"When you sign up to work at the White House, even as a civilian, part of your job is to defend the president," one unnamed White House reporter told the Post.
"That's not my job. I cover the president. Reporters take risks as part of the job, but not on behalf of the president."
The Wall Street Journal reported Israel had briefed the US about a possible shoulder-to-air missile strike on Air Force One, adding that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was among senior officials and staff who remained on the plane.
Dispatches sent by pool media on board noted a Secret Service order that window shades be lowered during takeoff – an unusual instruction outside of combat zones.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday called for Congress to be briefed "on the Iranian threats against the president, the extraordinary measures taken to get him out of Turkey."
Trump's trip to the Nato summit had already raised eyebrows after he arrived on a luxury Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar and retrofitted to carry the US president.
But it was reportedly not fitted with anti-missile security systems and the old Air Force One was called into action.
Trump claimed at the time that the new plane was being sent ahead for US troops in Britain to tour, as a treat.
At a stopover in Britain, he returned to the Qatar-gifted plane for the flight to Washington.
Asked at the time why journalists had been asked to lower window blinds he said "because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with."
"If I go, you go. Right?" Trump told reporters.
The White House has yet to respond directly to the alleged plane swap.
"There are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," Trump's communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
In 2000, Bill Clinton switched presidential planes at the last minute while traveling from India to Pakistan, using a decoy aircraft carrying Secret Service agents.
Joe Biden's 2023 visit to Ukraine was also shrouded in strict secrecy during a long journey by plane and train, though he was accompanied by a reporter and photographer.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 'Zombie city': Pereira reels from quake that killed 240
Article:
PEREIRA, Colombia: Jorge Gonzalez searches with his bare hands for his aunt under the ruins of a four-story building in Pereira, one of the cities hardest hit by the powerful earthquake in Colombia that has left at least 240 dead.
Like hundreds of volunteers and rescuers, he has spent hours clinging to the faintest hope there may be survivors in the rubble, despite the 7.4 magnitude quake that struck this coffee capital on Monday morning.
The 35-year-old works tirelessly on a small mountain of rubble, but it is increasingly unlikely he will find the woman he considers a mother alive.
Amid slabs of wall and masonry, he finds the bathroom "full of blood" on the floor where his aunt, 87-year-old Nubia Bonilla, lived.
"Since yesterday, I got here and I haven't left. Until they give me the body, I'm not leaving this place," Gonzalez tells AFP.
"She was all I had, and she's gone. Now I'm all alone," he adds, tears in his eyes.
All around him, the death toll rises with each passing hour.
By daybreak, residents were returning to their damaged homes to salvage some belongings before they collapsed completely.
Water and some food items were already running short in supermarkets and shops.
Almost all of Pereira was left without electricity, and the cell network is patchy at best.
- 'ZOMBIE CITY' -
The streets are littered with glass and chunks of brick.
It is a "zombie city," says 30-year-old resident Juan David Gaitan.
For Jesus Pineros, this earthquake has left him homeless for the second time.
Three years ago, he arrived in Colombia by bus, fleeing the crisis in neighboring Venezuela.
But the house where he lived with his siblings and nephews was reduced to pieces by the quake.
"As migrants, we've already been through some tough things back in our own country, and you never imagine something like this would happen on top of that," said the 28-year-old construction worker.
The family took refuge in a relative's house that remained standing.
Several children sleep on mattresses along the sidewalk in front of the home.
They tried to spend the night inside, but the roof groaned and terrified them.
Hundreds of homes collapsed or are cracked.
On the streets there are cars crushed by fallen walls and hanging power lines. Pineros sees the tragedy as a challenge for the family to rebuild their lives for the second time.
"We're starting from the bottom. We have to get back up again just like everyone else," he says.
- DEATH AND DESTRUCTION -
Stella Galvis recalls the moments of panic and the dust and how she ran with her child and husband seconds before her four-story building collapsed.
"We've been left with nothing. We lost everything," says the accountant, who lived on the ground floor, in tears.
"We were saved by a miracle," she adds.
Street vendor Maribel Verano, 46, is desperately searching for her missing mother and sister.
Both were in a small hotel that was reduced to rubble in a commercial area of the city.
Her mother, 72-year-old Luz Marina, recently suffered a thrombosis, and her sister Sandra, 38, ended up in a wheelchair because of meningitis.
"I hope to find them in good health," the woman says, unable to hide her sadness.
She is overwhelmed by memories of other nightmare disasters, such as the massive earthquake that shook the same region in 1999 and left nearly 1,200 dead.
And another that she lived through as a child: the 1985 eruption of the Nevado del Ruiz volcano, which wiped out an entire town called Armero and left 25,000 dead.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US, allies warn against unannounced missile launches
Article:
WASHINGTON: The United States and some 40 other countries warned Tuesday of the dangers of ballistic missile testing without advance notice, in a joint statement issued a month after China launched a nuclear-capable missile in the Pacific.
"Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests," said the joint statement issued by countries from Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
"It increases the risk of miscalculation, undermines global stability and security, and is incompatible with the responsibilities that come with possessing long-range missile capabilities," the countries said.
The statement called on all countries to provide at least 24 hours' notice of launches, including the class of missile being launched as well as the planned launch window, area and direction.
"Countries should also provide clear notices for airmen and mariners consistent with international standards to reduce risk, including in expected impact or landing areas," the statement added.
Beijing gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing an intercontinental ballistic missile last month, flexing its military might in a region where it has long sought to expand its reach.
The rocket appeared to land in a patch of ocean somewhere between the Solomon Islands, Nauru and Tuvalu, monitors have said.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US helicopter fired on ship that tried to break Iran ports blockade
Article:
WASHINGTON: A US helicopter on Tuesday fired missiles into the engine room of a Panama-flagged cargo ship that attempted to break the American blockade of Iran's ports, the United States military said.
The US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired on and disabled the M/V Vela Nova "after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on X, adding that the vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran in violation of the US blockade."
It was the third time the United States, in a months-long war against Iran, has forcibly halted a vessel since reinstating the ports blockade on July 14.
CENTCOM said it has redirected 55 ships that tried to run the blockade and boarded two others as of Tuesday.
US forces previously blockaded Iranian ports from April 13 to June 18, during which time they disabled nine ships and redirected more than 140, according to CENTCOM.
Iran has demanded that the United States end the ports blockade as part of its conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for oil and gas shipments before the war that has seen traffic plummet due to Teheran's attacks on ships in the area.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Taiwan's return to summit triggers Beijing warning
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
China warned a top Pacific Islands diplomat to "avoid affecting the healthy and stable development of ties" yesterday, after he said Taiwan would attend an annual meeting of the regional bloc's leaders.
The island was barred from the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting last year after protests from Beijing, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory.
Baron Waqa, the forum's secretary-general, said last Friday Taipei would attend this year.
"China urges the Pacific Islands Forum secretary to strictly adhere to the one-China principle, properly handle Taiwan-related issues and avoid affecting the healthy and stable development of ties between China and the forum," said Beijing's Foreign Ministry yesterday in response to an earlier AFP question about the matter.
Forum members Nauru, Kiribati and Solomon Islands have all cut diplomatic ties with Taipei since 2019, with the latter blocking Taiwan from attending the meeting when it hosted last year.
That resulted in all external countries being disinvited to the meeting, despite the island states' reliance on foreign aid and investment.
Palau, host of this year's event from Aug 30 to Sept 4, is among Taiwan's 12 remaining diplomatic partners.
"Taiwan is a very important development partner. It is not a dialogue partner, however it engages with members of our forum family," said Waqa after the ministers met in Fiji last week.
Along with Palau, forum members Tuvalu and Marshall Islands are also diplomatic partners of Taiwan.
On Friday, Pacific Island foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint response to China's missile launch last month, with further discussions expected at the Pacific leaders meeting at the end of the month, said New Zealand's foreign minister.
China's test-firing of a missile into the Pacific alarmed regional powers but failed to spur a unified response from Pacific Island governments.
Many of the foreign ministers and senior officials from the 18 countries represented at the Pacific Islands Forum meeting in Suva expressed concern to Reuters about the missile test.
However, New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said in Suva two members had refused to sign on to the statement, without giving a clear reason. He would not name the two countries.
An official with knowledge of the discussions said it was Nauru and Kiribati.

Title: Aratas invests RM259m in advanced manufacturing facility
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
KUALA LUMPUR: Aratas Corp, a member of the Omron Group, is investing about RM259 million to build an advanced manufacturing facility at COMPASS @ Kota Seri Langat, Selangor, as it expands production capacity to meet growing demand in India and the Asia-Pacific region.
Omron Malaysia Sdn Bhd, Aratas' manufacturing arm, selected the 6.87ha site after signing a sale and purchase agreement with COMPASS IP Sdn Bhd.
The new factory is expected to increase Aratas' production capacity by 1.5 times its current level, contributing more than 10 per cent of the group's total global production capacity.
Construction is scheduled to begin in October, subject to the necessary approvals, with completion and operations targeted by the end of 2027.
COMPASS IP director Datuk Stewart LaBrooy said the project highlighted the appeal of the industrial park as a location for multinational manufacturers seeking resilient infrastructure and sustainability credentials.
"What sets COMPASS apart is the marriage of sustainability and functionality. As Selangor's first green-rated managed industrial park, we provide multinationals with the infrastructure resilience, connectivity and ESG-aligned environment they need to future-proof their supply chains."
COMPASS is a joint venture between Permodalan Nasional Bhd, Area Group and KWEST Group.
The development comprises the COMPASS Industrial & Logistics Hub and the adjacent COMPASS SME Precinct, which was completed earlier this year and has achieved a strong take-up rate.

Title: Syed Saddiq: Don't burden future generations with fund's rescue
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
The financial burden of rescuing Tabung Haji must not be passed on to future generations and taxpayers, said Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman (Muda-Muar).
He criticised opposition members of parliament who yesterday boycotted the parliamentary debate on the pilgrimage fund's Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) report over the absence of Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
"If there are facts, debate. If there is wrongdoing, expose it.
"It is very unfortunate that we, on the opposition side, who are the loudest in championing the Malay-Muslim cause, have chosen to boycott the debate on the institution that is most important to the Malay-Muslim community," he said during the special Dewan Rakyat sitting on the RCI report.
"We are not boycotting the prime minister. We are boycotting our duty to millions of Tabung Haji depositors."
While agreeing that Anwar should respond to criticism over the government's handling of the Tabung Haji report and its recovery plan upon returning to Parliament, Syed Saddiq said his absence should not stall proceedings.
"Parliament is not a one-man show. The prime minister is unwell, but that does not mean the rest of us should stop doing our jobs."
Syed Saddiq said the issue was not merely the size of Tabung Haji's past investment losses, but whether the cost of rescuing and stabilising the institution would ultimately be borne by younger Malaysians and taxpayers.
"If there are losses and you continue paying high hibah, the money does not simply come from nowhere. We are transferring the burden from one generation to another."
He said young people and taxpayers had already borne more than RM10 billion in bailouts to save Tabung Haji, while questioning the government's commitment to the recommended RM1.7 billion annual fiscal injection under its recovery plan.
"On paper, yes, you saved Tabung Haji. But if you do not fulfil that responsibility, you are merely transferring the problem from one generation to the next and from one government to another," he said.
Syed Saddiq called for a multi-agency task force to investigate troubled investments, with the probe expanded to Felda, FGV Holdings Bhd and the Eagle High plantation deal.
He also urged amendments to the Tabung Haji Act 1995 to end political appointments and introduce a transparent, merit-based selection process.
He said action should be taken against those responsible for the fund's problems, regardless of political affiliation.
"Be bold, be brave, and do not take action only when it involves an enemy or a friend.
"The issue is not about me or you, friends or enemies. It is about the rights of more than 10 million depositors and the rights of Muslims in Malaysia," he added.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia steps up connectivity push
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
Malaysia is positioning itself as a more connected regional economy, with the expanded air links and its multiple growth corridors aimed at attracting investment from Hong Kong and beyond.
Transport Minister Anthony Loke said Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd was aiming to make Malaysia the most connected country in the Asia Pacific, backed by capacity expansion at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) and efforts to establish more direct international routes to Penang, Kota Kinabalu and Kuching.
He said stronger connectivity was essential for the movement of capital and goods, while helping deepen Malaysia's economic ties with major regional centres.
He said Kuala Lumpur and Hong Kong were less than four hours apart by air and shared the same time zone, with Cathay Pacific operating four daily services between the cities since March.
"There are four direct flights... just by Cathay Pacific, not counting other airlines. That tells us the commercial demand is growing," he said at the Think Business, Think Hong Kong symposium here yesterday.
He said KLIA had also collaborated with Henan Airport in Zhengzhou to develop a dual air cargo hub under the Air Silk Road concept.
"Our aim is to make KLIA our main cargo hub in the Asean region, while Hong Kong already has a strong presence in East Asia and strong connections to the United States and Canada."
Loke also urged Hong Kong investors to look beyond Kuala Lumpur and the Klang Valley, pointing to a multi-growth-corridor strategy offering opportunities across regions and industries.
In the north, he identified Penang and Kulim as key semiconductor and electronics corridors, while Johor offered opportunities through the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone.
He said the 665km East Coast Rail Link, with its first phase expected to be completed next year, would boost manufacturing and connect the region with the Klang Valley.
Sarawak offered opportunities in renewable and green energy, while Sabah had potential in tourism and the blue economy, he added.
Loke said Malaysia was also seeking to move further up the value chain under the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, focusing on advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, the digital economy and energy transition.
"We have become more selective about the investments we court, because the objective now is quality and long-term capability."
The symposium brought together more than 200 government and business leaders, startup entrepreneurs and professional service providers from Hong Kong and Malaysia.
Present were Hong Kong Trade Development Council chairman Professor Frederick Ma and Hong Kong Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau.

Title: Air India captain's confirmatory drug test positive for marijuana, source says
Article:
NEW DELHI: The captain of an Air India Phuket-Delhi flight that suddenly lost about 91.44 metres (300 feet) of altitude last week has tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test, a source familiar with the matter said.
Earlier in the day, India's Ministry of Civil Aviation summoned Air India CEO Campbell Wilson over the incident, which involved an Airbus A320neo aircraft, a second source said.
Air India and the ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Wilson told news channels the airline had briefed the ministry on the status of the investigation into the incident.
The summons came days after Indian authorities opened an investigation into the incident, which injured 13 passengers and four crew members.
The flight from the Thai tourist city experienced a "momentary altitude variation" while it was flying over the eastern Indian state of Odisha, the government had said earlier.
The aircraft, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members, landed safely in Delhi. On Sunday, the Ministry of Civil Aviation said the captain's initial screening for psychoactive substances produced a result requiring confirmatory laboratory testing.
Air India had said that it had not been informed of the results. The airline is majority-owned by the Tata Group, with Singapore Airlines holding a roughly 25 per cent stake.

Title: US rights groups sue Trump over ICC sanctions
Article:
NEW YORK: Rights groups on Tuesday sued US President Donald Trump over his sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court, saying the measures block victims of war crimes from pursuing justice.
The Trump administration, which rejects the ICC's authority, has imposed travel bans and asset freezes on several judges and prosecutors, primarily over their investigations into key US ally Israel.
In a New York court filing, four groups including Human Rights Watch said the sanctions should be struck down as they violate laws including First Amendment free speech protections.
"This is an unlawful abuse of power constituting a frontal attack on the rule of law, the independence of judges, prosecutors, and lawyers, basic precepts undergirding the international legal order, and the principle of equal access to justice," the lawsuit states.
The 101-page complaint says the restrictions "cause grave damage to the ability to bring to justice the perpetrators of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity."
The US sanctions, issued under an executive order Trump signed in February 2025, have targeted eight judges, three prosecutors, a UN expert and three human rights organizations.
The United Nations and the European Union previously urged Trump to reverse penalties against ICC officials.
Many of the measures were directly linked to an arrest warrant that The Hague-based court issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the war in Gaza.
Washington has also criticised ICC probes into alleged abuses during the US-led war in Afghanistan.
Tuesday's complaint, filed by HRW, American Friends Service Committee, Center for Constitutional Rights and Open Society Institute, says the sanctions have caused "profound and irreparable harm."
It states that the four groups have been forced to stop fully engaging with the ICC due to fears of civil or criminal penalties, and of being designated for sanctions themselves.
Alongside Trump, the lawsuit names Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Bradley Smith, director of the Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Established in 2002, the ICC prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.
US reservations about the court predate Trump. The US, like Israel, has not ratified the international treaty that established the ICC, which is backed by nearly all Western democracies.
Russia is also not a member. Its President Vladimir Putin has been the subject of an ICC arrest warrant since March 2023.
Washington vowed last month to accelerate its campaign against the ICC beyond the existing sanctions – accusing the court of posing "an intolerable threat to US sovereignty."
A State Department official told AFP the effort would look to pressure other nations to withdraw from the court and cut off any financial support to the court.
In June, three ICC judges sanctioned by the Trump administration filed a lawsuit against the president and other senior US officials, arguing that the measures imposed on them were unlawful.
In a complaint filed in New York, Canadian judge Kimberly Prost, Uganda's Solomy Balungi Bossa and Benin's Reine Adelaide Sophie Alapini-Gansou said the sanctions were intended to "exert extrajudicial pressure."

Title: Assad ruled Syria with iron fist before defeat in civil war
Article:
BASHAR al-Assad's 24-year rule of Syria ended abruptly in December 2024 following a lightning advance by rebel forces who struck while the Russian and Iranian allies who had backed him through years of civil war were distracted by conflicts elsewhere.
He fled to Moscow, ending more than five decades of iron-fisted rule by his family and opening a new chapter for Syria.
The historic shift was underscored on Tuesday when a Damascus court sentenced him to death in his absence for crimes including killings, arbitrary arrests and torture during the years in which he clung to power.
Assad became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez.
Shaped in its early years by the Iraq war and crisis in Lebanon, Assad's rule was defined by the civil war, which spiralled out of the 2011 Arab Spring, when Syrians demanding democracy took to the streets, to be met with deadly force.
Assad turned the full power of the Syrian military against his opponents as he sought to crush the rebellion inspired by the Arab Spring movement that had toppled leaders in Egypt and Tunisia.
Inquiries by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and the United Nations concluded that government forces under Assad used the nerve agent sarin and chlorine as a weapon in attacks during the civil war on rebel-held areas.
Following one poison gas attack in 2018, then-US President Donald Trump declared Assad an "animal." Authorities denied using chemical weapons, which killed and injured thousands during the war.
His ruthless approach to fighting rebels, including siege warfare tactics condemned as "medieval" by UN investigators, drew comparisons with the way his father had defeated Islamist insurgents in the 1980s.
Justifying his response, Assad compared himself to a surgeon cutting into a wound. "Do we say to him: 'your hands are covered in blood?' Or do we thank him for saving the patient?" he said in parliament in 2012.
Hundreds of thousands of people were killed in the war, cities were flattened, and more than a quarter of the population fled abroad.
A CRUMBLING ARMY
His grip on power appeared to be slipping in the first years of the war, as much of Syria fell to insurgents, some of them backed by Turkiye, Gulf Arab states and the United States.
Shia militias backed by his ally Iran began arriving in 2012 to fight on his side, shoring up his hold on Damascus. The arrival of Russia's air force in 2015 allowed Assad to go on the offensive and claw back the bulk of the country.
He outlasted many of the foreign leaders who believed his demise was imminent in the early days of the conflict.
But reliant on Moscow and Teheran for military support and with parts of Syria still beyond his grasp, Assad's rule remained precarious.
In late 2024, insurgents seized a moment of opportunity, attacking when Iran had been weakened by conflict with Israel and Russia was distracted by its war in Ukraine.
[[nid:1509167]]
Syria's demoralised army crumbled as rebels led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Islamist Hayat Tahrir al-Sham group swept towards Damascus.
Assad left the capital, first to a Russian airbase in Latakia, before being evacuated to Moscow on Dec 8, 2024.
'STATE-RUN MACHINERY OF DEATH'
Prisoners freed from Syria's notorious jails recounted the torture and abuse they'd endured.
An international war crimes prosecutor, visiting Syria after Assad was toppled, said evidence emerging from mass grave sites exposed a "state-run machinery of death."
He accused the Assad-led state of having conducted organised killing comparable to Nazi Germany.
In October 2025, Reuters revealed that the Assad government had secretly moved thousands of bodies to a site in the desert east of Damascus, to hide evidence of atrocities.
From the start, Assad described the conflict as an international conspiracy against a country that had stood in opposition to the United States and its Middle Eastern allies, especially Israel.
He characterised the rebels as foreign-backed Islamist extremists who would have been easily defeated were it not for their supporters overseas.
He dismissed the idea that there was such a thing as a moderate Syrian opposition.
After Sharaa, a former al Qaeda commander, seized power in Damascus, Assad issued a written statement saying that "the state had fallen into the hands of terrorism."
BARREL BOMBS
Assad hailed from Syria's Alawite minority, a group which follows a religion that is an offshoot of Shia Islam and had historically been based in Syria's coastal region.
Along with the presidency, he also inherited the leadership of the Syrian branch of the Baath Party, an Arab nationalist movement established in the 1940s.
Assad publicly held fast to the idea of Syria as a bastion of secular Arab nationalism even as the conflict appeared ever more sectarian, pitting his Alawite-led state and its Shia backer Iran against insurgents drawn from the Sunni Muslim majority and supported by Sunni-led states.
The use of chemical weapons against rebel-held areas of Syria marked some of the most extensive uses of poison gas since World War One.
The deadliest such attack was on rebel-held Ghouta in 2013. The attack with sarin gas killed hundreds of people. It prompted no Western military response.
[[nid:1509166]]
The threat of a US missile strike was averted when Moscow brokered a deal for Syria's chemical weapons to be destroyed by the following year.
After another sarin attack, in 2017, Trump ordered a cruise missile strike on a Syrian air base.
Earlier this year, the transitional leadership that took power after Assad was toppled said it had located remnants of a clandestine chemical weapons programme, including raw materials and munitions similar to those used to carry out deadly gas attacks during the civil war.
Assad consistently denied accusations that the state was to blame, in one instance accusing the global chemical weapons watchdog of fabricating a report about the use of chlorine gas at Washington's behest, echoing a broader pattern of rejecting allegations of state brutality.
In a BBC interview in 2015, he appeared to make light of accusations that the army was dropping barrel bombs – barrels packed with explosives that cause indiscriminate destruction – saying:
"I haven't heard of the army using barrels, or maybe, cooking pots."
When tens of thousands of photos were smuggled out of Syria showing brutal torture of people in government custody, Assad dismissed it as part of a plot funded by Qatar.
In 2025, France issued an arrest warrant for Assad and other former Syrian officials over the bombing of a press centre in the city of Homs in 2012.
EYE DOCTOR
Assad hadn't always been destined for the presidency: Hafez had groomed another son, Bassel, for the role.
But when Bassel died in a car crash in 1994, Bashar was transformed from an eye doctor in London - where he studied as a postgraduate - to heir apparent.
The early days of his rule gave rise to cautious optimism about reform in Syria, where a feared security apparatus had underpinned Hafez al-Assad's rule since 1971.
But this hope soon evaporated. The police state remained intact, perpetuating repression that ultimately fuelled the uprising against his rule in 2011.
Dissidents were jailed and economic reforms contributed to what US diplomats described, in a 2008 embassy cable released by WikiLeaks, as "parasitic" nepotism and corruption.
While the elite did well, drought was driving the poor from rural areas to slums where the revolt would blaze.
He is married to  British-born former investment banker, Asma Akhras, with whom he has three children.
* The article is from Reuters
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Ocalan is founder of Kurdish PKK and also author of its end
Article:
ABDULLAH   Ocalan, jailed founder of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and an icon for many Kurds but a reviled terrorist for many Turks,  is now at the heart of the biggest push for peace in over a decade.
The group's leader, who oversaw decades of violence against the Turkish state, last year threw his weight behind a bid to end decades of armed conflict, with fighters from his PKK accepting his call to disarm.
On Monday, Turkish lawmakers voted through a bill offering limited amnesty for certain PKK fighters, in a first legislative step towards ending a conflict that caused some 50,000 deaths.
Crucially, the legislation turned a blind eye to the fate of Ocalan, 77, who since 1999 has been serving life in solitary confinement on the prison island of Imrali near Istanbul.
"I believe in the power of politics and social peace, not weapons. And I call on you to put this principle into practice," he said in July last year as PKK leaders began symbolically destroying their weapons.
Since the latest tentative moves began in October 2024, PKK leaders demanded Ocalan's release as essential for the process to work.
"He is the person who initiated this process," said senior PKK leader Devrim Palu in October.
"His freedom is crucial for this process to advance with greater effectiveness."
For many Turks, Ocalan, who founded the PKK in 1978 and embodies the Kurdish rebellion, is the No. 1 public enemy.
A Marxist-inspired group, the PKK began an insurgency in 1984, demanding independence and later broader autonomy in Turkiye's mostly Kurdish southeast.
It was quickly blacklisted as a "terror" organisation by Ankara and many Western nations.
Attitudes began shifting in October 2024 when Ocalan responded positively to an olive branch offered by Devlet Bahceli, a close ally of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The Kurds  were left without a country when the Ottoman Empire collapsed after World War 1, and  most live in Turkiye but they are also spread across Syria, Iraq and Iran.
[[nid:1509162]]
Ocalan was born into a mixed Turkish-Kurdish peasant family in Turkiye's southeast on April 4, 1949.
He became a left-wing activist while studying politics at university in Ankara and set up the PKK in 1978.
Six years later, Ocalan oversaw its shift to armed struggle, then spent years on the run, fleeing first to Syria, where he stayed until he was forced to run again in 1998.
In search of a haven, he ended up at the Greek consulate in Kenya, where Turkish agents snatched him in an operation on Feb 15, 1999.
Sentenced to death, he escaped the gallows when Turkiye began abolishing capital punishment in 2002 and has since been held on Imrali.
For many Kurds, he is a hero whom they call "Apo" — Kurdish for "uncle". But Turks have called him "bebek katili" (baby killer) due to the PKK's ruthless tactics.
But even from his cell, Ocalan continued to lead, ordering a ceasefire that lasted from 1999 until 2004.
In 2005, he ordered followers to renounce the idea of an independent Kurdish state and campaign for autonomy in their respective countries.
Ocalan was involved in more talks in 2013 when Erdogan was premier, but those collapsed in July 2015, sparking a particularly deadly outbreak of violence.
Although that eventually tailed off, there were no further efforts at dialogue until this latest bid.
Since then, Ocalan has been regularly visited by a small delegation from the pro-Kurdish DEM party.
Ahead of the vote, he sent back a message of hope.
"With this law, we are setting out to solve a historical problem. We are at the start of a democratisation process that will be at least as important as the founding of the Republic," he said of Turkiye's founding in 1923.
"It is now necessary to work with the same seriousness for a democratic republic."
* The writer is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 'Spirit of Anchorage' a shadow of itself one year after summit
Article:
TRUMP-PUTIN TALKS
IN the year since Donald Trump hosted Vladimir Putin in the United States for a summit designed to broker an end to Russia's offensive on Ukraine, the diplomatic initiative has fizzled out and the conflict has escalated.
For months, Russian officials talked up the "spirit of Anchorage" — a supposed climate of detente, renewed dialogue with Washington and a framework for finding a way out of the  conflict.
Now there are few traces of that atmosphere. US mediation efforts are at a standstill, Russia and Ukraine are ramping up attacks and more civilians are being killed than at any point since the first months of the war.
On Aug 15 last year, Trump broke with the West's policy of isolating Putin, rolling out the red carpet as the Kremlin chief stepped off his plane at the Elmendorf-Richardson airbase in Alaska.
It remains unclear what was decided behind closed doors.
Russia has always maintained some kind of understanding that a peace deal was struck — "a compromise proposal", as Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov called it.
Washington has rebuffed any talk of a deal being reached.
"There was a proposal in  Alaska, but there was no  agreement. If there had been an  agreement, we would have had an end of the war," said Secretary of State Marco Rubio in June.
Moscow had hoped the summit would lay the foundations for a "lasting peace" by addressing what it calls the "root causes" of the conflict, said political analyst Sergei Markov — designated a "foreign agent" but still close to the Russian authorities.
For years — including right before launching its offensive in February 2022 — Russia has called for a new overarching security deal with the US over Europe, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation  and arms control.
The "compromise" Russia tabled in Alaska, said Markov, was to limit its territorial claims on Ukraine to the eastern Donbas region in exchange for recognition of Russia's new borders by Washington and the lifting of sanctions.
Those Russian demands were included in a 28-point document drafted by the US — later cut down to 19 — after separate negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow.
The document was never published officially and never came to fruition.
US-brokered direct talks between Russia and Ukraine early this year broke down, chiefly over the issue of territory.
Ukraine refuses to cede land it still controls and wants an immediate ceasefire along the current frontline, with territorial status to be decided during fuller peace talks.
And since late February, Washington's attention has been consumed by the war on Iran.
Trump has since issued fresh sanctions on Russia and the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement — New Start — has been allowed to lapse.
Russia has lately allowed itself to publicly question Washington's commitment to diplomacy.
"I don't even want to imagine that Alaska... was conceived to gain time in order to strengthen Ukraine militarily," said Lavrov in June.
A meeting between Lavrov and Rubio in Manila last month — their first since last September — lasted only around 30 minutes.
"We'll have to find new suggestions and new ideas" that both "Russia and Ukraine can agree to", said Rubio after that meeting.
The two sides' conditions for peace are irreconcilable. Russia demands territory alongside political and military concessions that Ukraine rejects as capitulation.
At the same time, both are convinced force can improve their negotiating position.
"The Russian armed forces will continue their mission to liberate the Donbas and Novorossiya in line with the approved plan," Russia's army chief Valery Gerasimov told Putin in a televised meeting early last month – referring to land stretching across eastern and southern Ukraine.
Buoyed by European support, Kyiv is banking on its long-range strike campaign to tip Russia's economy and society over the edge.
Russia has upped its missile attacks on Kyiv, killing dozens there in recent weeks.
It has also brought Ukrainian exports through the Black Sea to a standstill through a campaign of port and ship strikes.
"The spirit of Anchorage has dissipated," said Russian political analyst Fyodor Lukyanov — close to the ruling elite — this month.
The result? "Brutal escalation."

Title: Man arrested over alleged machete robbery of elderly woman in Ipoh
Article:
IPOH: A 32-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly robbing an elderly woman at a house in Langkap near Teluk Intan.
Hilir Perak District Police chief ACP Chua Kok Lian said police received a report from the 69-year-old woman, who claimed she had been robbed by an unidentified man.
He said the incident occurred at 4am, when the suspect, who was armed with a machete, allegedly snatched a gold bracelet worn by the victim, causing her to sustain injuries. The loss was estimated at RM6,000.
"Following the report, further investigations and intelligence led to the arrest of a 32-year-old man at 2.30am today in Slim River.
"Police also recovered and seized a gold bracelet believed to be linked to the case for further investigation," he said in a statement tonight.
Chua said the suspect was remanded for seven days until Aug 17 to assist investigations under Section 394 of the Penal Code for causing hurt while committing a robbery.
In a separate statement, Chua said two men suspected of being linked to a break-in at a fishing equipment shop on Jalan Changkat Jong, Teluk Intan, had also been arrested.
He said police received a report from the shop owner after the premises was found prised open and broken into on July 30, with an inspection revealing that fishing equipment worth about RM8,000 was missing.
"Following the report, police conducted investigations and intelligence operations before arresting two males aged 13 and 19 in separate raids.
"Further investigations also led police to recover and seize several items believed to be linked to the case for further investigation," he said, adding that both suspects would be charged under Section 414 of the Penal Code at the Teluk Intan magistrate's court tomorrow.

Title: NST Leader: Housing policies must put people before numbers
Article:
THE government deserves credit for moving beyond merely announcing new projects and addressing the legacy problem of abandoned developments. For decades, stalled projects have scarred communities and left buyers financially and emotionally burdened.
The recent recovery efforts show that intervention, when backed by political will and coordination, can deliver results. However, the true test lies not in setting targets but in ensuring that they are achieved.
One way to do this is to build where demand exists. A simple idea that makes great economic sense but is seldom adhered to.
Affordable housing should not become affordable only because it is located far from jobs, public transport and amenities. Data-driven planning must remain central to housing, not developers' or policymakers' whims and fancies.
Rehabilitation is commendable, but prevention is better. Stronger financial screening of developers, stricter project monitoring and earlier intervention mechanisms are needed to stop projects from becoming distressed in the first place.
Financial solvency of developers is one of the major issues in Malaysia with many facing cash-flow problems: not enough capital to pay contractors, suppliers or finance companies. How their projects get the stamp of the authorities or finance companies is a mystery.
Project feasibility is an issue as well. When costs associated with construction, land or financing are underestimated or when houses are priced excessively the project becomes commercially unviable.
Malaysia is in an unfortunate position because when a project is legally approved with purchasers having paid substantial sums, it can still get stalled should the developer be unable to finance construction. Or disputes arise between the developers, contractors and banks leading to  long legal battles that leave purchasers financially and emotionally drained.
For sure, projects can be stalled or even abandoned when  developers are financially solvent. A thorough study on the underlying cause of project failure is needed. Abandoned housing projects are just symptoms.
Another preventive measure is to strengthen transparency and accountability, two areas where Malaysia scores low. Progress towards the one-million-home target should be publicly tracked through regular reporting.
Malaysians should be able to see how many units are completed, occupied and delivered to the intended beneficiaries.
Another is to focus on livability, not just numbers. A million homes is an impressive figure, but success should also be measured by whether families can build sustainable lives in these communities.
Then there is an issue with the word  "affordability". Affordable to whom? To developers? To policymakers? Everyone but the buyers. Affordability mustn't be just in the eye of the beholder, changing as the beholder changes.
The government must ensure that affordability is genuine. Housing prices must be aligned with local incomes, not merely labelled "affordable". Home ownership should not force households into unsustainable debt.

Title: No by-election for Subang after Wong Chen's resignation - EC
Article:
